Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette: Mr. Tran's eyes still scan the room with a mix of caution and hypervigilance, even in the quiet confines of his therapist's office. It's been decades since he fled the war-torn streets of Saigon, but the memories remain as vivid as ever. He recalls the day American forces pulled out, leaving behind chaos and destruction. Mr. Tran, then a young man, found himself caught in the crossfire, hiding from the advancing North Vietnamese Army. In the mayhem, he was pinned beneath the rubble of a destroyed building, unable to move or escape. The smell of smoke and burning rubber instantly transports him back to that moment. It's as if no time has passed at all - his heart racing, his breath catching in his throat. The olfactory trigger is potent enough that even walking past a construction site can send him reeling. He tries to explain it to himself: "It's just my brain playing tricks," but the fear feels too real, too visceral. In the years following the war, Mr. Tran built a new life in America, working as a warehouse worker and living a quiet, solitary existence. However, the memories never fully receded. Whenever he recalls that day, the emotions come flooding back - grief, helplessness, and above all, fear. He's learned to recognize the warning signs: his mind starts racing, his palms grow sweaty, and he feels an overwhelming urge to flee. Confrontations of any kind can also send him spiraling back into the past. A disagreement with a coworker or even a stern word from a supervisor is enough to make him feel like he's reliving those moments of being pinned down, helpless. He tries to sidestep conflicts whenever possible, knowing that his reactions will only escalate the situation. The physical sensation of feeling restrained or held down can trigger an intense panic response in Mr. Tran. Even something as mundane as getting a blood pressure test at the doctor's office can set him off. The touch of the cuff on his arm is enough to transport him back to those moments of being trapped beneath the rubble. Despite his best efforts, Mr. Tran has grown increasingly isolated over the years. He stopped attending family gatherings and cultural events, unable to bear the sounds and smells that might trigger another episode. His job at the warehouse has become a lonely, monotonous routine - he goes through the motions, always on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Lately, Mr. Tran's avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his physical health. He's been experiencing chronic pain and stiffness in his joints, which his doctor attributes to years of accumulated stress. The breaking point came when his supervisor threatened to let him go due to excessive absenteeism - a stark reminder that his struggles are no longer just internal. As he sits in the therapist's office, Mr. Tran finally feels ready to confront the demons he's been running from for so long. He knows it won't be easy, but he hopes to find some measure of peace, some way to quiet the memories and live a life free from the constant threat of being pulled back into the past. For now, though, the fear remains - a persistent whisper in his ear: "What if I'm not strong enough? What if it all comes flooding back?"
